About the Lodge

141 Years of Brotherhood in West Texas

Staked Plains Lodge No. 598 was chartered on December 12, 1884, under the Grand Lodge of Texas, A.F. & A.M. For more than a century, we have met on the South Main Street in Big Spring — the same community we have served since the Permian Basin was open range.

In 1885, Lodge members helped establish what would become Mount Olive Cemetery, one of the oldest burial grounds in Howard County. That act of civic responsibility is characteristic of who we are: a fraternity that takes seriously its obligation to the place it calls home.

What Is Freemasonry

A Brotherhood Built on Timeless Principles

Freemasonry is believed to be the world's oldest fraternal organization. It brings together men of good character — across every background, profession, and walk of life — in a shared commitment to personal growth, mutual support, and service to community.

What happens inside our Lodge room belongs to the Brethren. What you will find outside it is men who take that experience seriously.

Brotherly Love

Freemasonry teaches us to regard all mankind as one family — to treat others with kindness, respect, patience, and understanding, even when we disagree. It is a principle that extends beyond the Lodge room into every relationship a Mason carries in daily life.

Relief

Relief is more than charity. It is the duty to assist those in distress — whether that need is physical, emotional, financial, or spiritual — while expecting nothing in return. Every Mason carries this obligation to his Brethren, their families, and his broader community.

Truth

Truth calls us to pursue honesty, integrity, and moral courage in all things. It demands that a Mason be truthful with others and with himself — and that the search for wisdom and self-improvement never stop. It is not a quality a man arrives at. It is one he works toward his entire life.

Freemasonry has been practiced in Texas since the Republic. Among its members: Sam Houston, Stephen F. Austin, and Mirabeau B. Lamar. The tradition continues in Big Spring.

Service & Giving

Masonic Charities

Texas Masons support a broad network of charitable programs — many operated statewide, all funded without public solicitation.

  • Masonic Children & Family Services of Texas
  • Texas Scottish Rite Hospital for Children
  • Shriner's Hospitals for Children
  • Texas Masonic Retirement Community
  • DeMolay International
  • Rainbow Girls & Job's Daughters
Staked Plains Lodge in the Community
Fantastic Teeth Fan Club

Each year, Lodge members deliver free dental hygiene kits to first graders at Big Spring elementary schools — part of a statewide program that has reached over 1.4 million Texas children.

Mirabeau B. Lamar Award of Excellence

Annual recognition for outstanding Big Spring educators, presented at the Howard County school district's awards ceremony. Named for Mirabeau B. Lamar — Mason, President of the Republic of Texas, and Father of Texas Education.

Teachers Appreciation Dinner

Lodge members host and cook an annual dinner for Big Spring educators at the lodge hall — a personal expression of the fraternity's historic commitment to public education.

Annual Senior Scholarships

Scholarships awarded to graduating Big Spring seniors through an essay competition. Candidates' essays are read in open Lodge; recipients are selected by vote of the Brethren.

Becoming a Mason

The Path to Membership

Freemasonry does not recruit. A man comes to us of his own free will, drawn by genuine curiosity and a desire to improve himself. If that describes you, the process below is how it begins. It is not a quick process — and that is by design.

To petition, a man must be:
At least 18 years of age Of good moral character A belief in a Supreme Being Free of felony convictions A resident of the Lodge jurisdiction
1
Reach Out

Contact the Lodge through our website, email, or Facebook — or simply show up. Our dinners are open to the public, and some of the best first conversations happen around a table. However you find us, that first step costs nothing and obligates you to nothing.

2
Get to Know the Lodge

Before submitting a petition, spend time getting acquainted with the Brethren. Ask questions. Attend a public event. Get a genuine sense of who we are and whether this is right for you. This works both ways — we want to know you as well. We are not looking to add names to a membership roll. We are looking for men we hope to one day call Brother.

3
Submit a Petition

When you are ready, you complete and submit a petition to the Lodge. The petition asks for basic information about your background, your character, and your reasons for seeking membership.

4
Petition Read Before the Lodge

At the next Stated Meeting, your petition is read in its entirety before the Brethren, ensuring every member has the opportunity to become familiar with you before the process moves forward.

5
Investigation Committee

The Worshipful Master appoints three Master Masons to investigate your petition. Their task is to determine whether you possess the character and qualifications expected of a Freemason — not to judge your wealth or circumstances, but to know your character.

6
The Investigation

The committee will meet with you — typically in your home, and ideally with your family present. As the Grand Lodge of Texas puts it, no Mason is perfect, and no petitioner is expected to be. The purpose is honest conversation: answer your questions, help your family understand what Freemasonry asks, and allow the Brethren to know the man behind the petition. It is less an interrogation than an introduction.

7
Committee Report and Ballot

The committee reports its findings to the Lodge. The Brethren then vote by secret ballot — a longstanding tradition that allows every member to vote according to his conscience. You will be notified of the result.

8
The Degrees

If elected, you begin your journey through the three degrees of Freemasonry: Entered Apprentice, Fellow Craft, and Master Mason. Each degree is a distinct experience. What you find there is meant to be lived, not described in advance.

What This Looks Like in Practice
Month One
You reach out, meet some of the Brethren, and decide to petition. Your petition is submitted and read at the Stated Meeting.
Month Two
The Worshipful Master appoints your investigation committee. The Brethren contact you promptly to schedule visits, conducted at your home with family present.
Month Three
The committee reports to the Lodge. The ballot is taken. If elected, you are contacted and preparations begin for your Entered Apprentice Degree.

This timeline is approximate. The Lodge moves at a pace that serves both the petitioner and the Brethren — what it will not do is rush a decision that carries this much weight on either side.

It has been said among Masons that the investigation is like a first degree — the first opportunity for the petitioner and the Lodge to truly know one another.
